title: Denim Sculptures That Unravel the American Dream
summary: Denim is more than just a fabric—it's a symbol of American culture, from the rugged cowboy to the rebellious James Dean. But artist Nick Doyle digs deeper. In his solo exhibition Collective Hallucinations at Perrotin gallery in New York, Doyle creates large wall sculptures entirely from layers of denim. His works include aviator sunglasses reflecting clouds, a Rocky Mountain landscape framed by brick, and even a life-sized fortune teller's shop. Doyle's fascination with denim began in 2018 when he found a roll of discarded denim in the trash. "At the time, I had no money, so I was making work out of material I found in the garbage," he shares. That chance discovery led him to explore the material's complex history: denim's roots in chattel slavery (when enslaved people dyed cotton with indigo), its association with Manifest Destiny and the gold rush, and its role in shaping American masculinity. For Doyle, denim embodies the contradictions of American life—the gap between the myth of the American Dream and the reality. "The world's image of America has changed, but our country's nostalgia for itself is making us late to the party," he says. The exhibition, which runs through May 30, presents these themes in varying shades of blue. If you're in New York, it's a thought-provoking look at what our clothes really say about us.
why_it_matters: This exhibition reveals how everyday objects like jeans carry deep and often painful histories, encouraging young people to think critically about the symbols they encounter daily and the stories behind them.

background_read: Denim originated in the French city of Nîmes (hence 'de Nîmes') and became sturdy workwear for American laborers in the 19th century. It gained rebellious cool through figures like James Dean (the actor who starred in 'Rebel Without a Cause' in the 1950s).
The indigo dye used in early denim was often cultivated by enslaved people on Southern plantations, which ties the fabric directly to the brutal history of chattel slavery in the Americas.
During the 1849 California Gold Rush, denim pants became essential for miners, and the ideology of Manifest Destiny drove rapid westward expansion across the continent.
Nick Doyle's exhibition is held at Perrotin gallery, an influential contemporary art gallery founded in Paris that now has spaces in New York, Tokyo, and elsewhere.

perspectives.description: Doyle's work creatively recycles denim to expose hidden histories, giving new life to discarded material and sparking important conversations about identity and memory.
Some viewers might find the sculptures overly bleak or see them as an unfair attack on American traditions, preferring art that focuses on unity rather than unresolved historical wounds.
Doyle follows a long line of contemporary artists who use ordinary consumer products to critique society, similar to how Andy Warhol used soup cans to comment on mass culture.
The exhibition could inspire more sustainable art practices and lead museums and schools to incorporate similar discussions about the hidden meanings of everyday materials.
